title: Who reports to whom
brief: We hired a lot this year and I keep getting asked who reports to whom. I want a plain list: each person and their manager. I have no manager, so leave mine empty.

skill.title: A table can join itself
skill.card: manager_id points at another row of the same table. Give the table two aliases and join them like two tables. A LEFT JOIN keeps the people without a manager.
skill.example: SELECT e.name, m.name AS boss FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id LIMIT 3;

task: Return employee (the name) and manager (the manager name) for every employee. The CEO appears with a NULL manager.
starter:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.manager_id AS manager
FROM employees e;
hint: Join employees to itself: LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id.

title: Who owes us a decision?
brief: I want to email every customer who has an order still pending. One email per customer, not one per order, so no duplicates please.

skill.title: Subqueries: a query inside a query
skill.card: A query in parentheses can feed another: WHERE x > (SELECT AVG(x) ...) compares with one value, WHERE id IN (SELECT ...) tests membership, EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...) checks that a match exists.
skill.example: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);

task: Return the name and email of customers who have at least one order with status pending. Each customer once. Use a subquery.
solution:
SELECT name, email FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending');
hint: WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending')

title: Add the department
brief: The list went around and everyone loved it. One more thing: put the department name on each line. Some people have no department, like me and our consultant, keep us in.
task: Return employee, department (the department name) and manager for every employee. Missing departments and managers stay NULL.
solution:
SELECT e.name AS employee, d.name AS department, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id;
hint: One more LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id, and d.name AS department between the two columns.

title: Revenue by month
brief: The board pack needs a revenue line per month. I keep rebuilding it by hand in a spreadsheet. Cancelled orders do not count, obviously.

skill.title: WITH names a step
skill.card: WITH name AS (SELECT ...) builds a temporary table you query right after, so a long report reads in steps. strftime('%Y-%m', date) gives the month, julianday(a) - julianday(b) a gap in days.
skill.example: WITH paid AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) SELECT * FROM paid WHERE total > 1000;

task: With a CTE, return month (YYYY-MM from ordered) and revenue (sum of qty * unit_price, rounded to 2 decimals) for orders that are not cancelled, ordered by month.
solution:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered) AS month, oi.qty * oi.unit_price AS amount
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
)
SELECT month, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue FROM lines GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;
hint: In the CTE use strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered) AS month, then GROUP BY month outside.

title: Salary rank inside each department
brief: Pay review is coming. I want to see every person with their rank inside their own department and the department average next to it, without losing the individual lines.

skill.title: Window functions keep every row
skill.card: fn() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x) computes across related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY. RANK(), ROW_NUMBER(), LAG(col) and any aggregate work as window functions.
skill.example: SELECT name, category, price, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC) AS r FROM products;

task: Return name, dept_id, salary, rank_in_dept (RANK by salary, highest = 1, within the same dept_id) and dept_avg (average salary of the department, rounded to 2 decimals). Skip employees with no dept_id.
solution:
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank_in_dept,
       ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id), 2) AS dept_avg
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL;
hint: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC), and AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id).

title: Add the order count and a running total
brief: The board liked the monthly line. They now want to see how many orders made each month, and the revenue so far in the year, so they can see the curve.
task: Return month, orders (number of distinct non cancelled orders that month), revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) and running (revenue of that month and all earlier months, rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by month.
solution:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered) AS month, o.id AS order_id, oi.qty * oi.unit_price AS amount
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
), months AS (
    SELECT month, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM lines GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month, orders, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 2) AS running
FROM months ORDER BY month;
hint: Keep o.id in the first CTE, group in a second CTE, then SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) for the running total.

title: Reporting lines for the directory
brief: I am building the staff directory in our intranet. For each person I need their depth in the org chart and their full chain of command as one text, like a breadcrumb.

skill.title: Recursive CTEs walk trees
skill.card: A WITH RECURSIVE query has an anchor (the starting rows), UNION ALL, then a step that reads the rows found so far. It repeats until the step finds nothing new: perfect for org charts.
skill.example: WITH RECURSIVE n(x) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5) SELECT x FROM n;

task: Return name, level (CEO = 0, direct reports 1, and so on) and path: the names from the CEO down to the person, joined by ' > ', for example Claire Durand > Nina Dubois > Yanis Bernard. Order by path.
solution:
WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, name, level, path) AS (
    SELECT id, name, 0, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, c.level + 1, c.path || ' > ' || e.name
    FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, level, path FROM chain ORDER BY path;
hint: Recursive step: join employees e on e.manager_id = c.id, level c.level + 1, path c.path || ' > ' || e.name.

title: Book in the delivery
brief: The truck just left. Three things for the system: we now sell a desk lamp, eight standing desks came in, and printer ink is discontinued so drop it from the catalogue. Its old order lines were archived this morning.

skill.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE change data
skill.card: INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (...) adds a row, UPDATE t SET col = ... WHERE ... changes rows, DELETE FROM t WHERE ... removes them. Without WHERE they hit every row, so run the matching SELECT first.
skill.example: SELECT name, stock FROM products WHERE name = 'Standing Desk';

task: Three statements. Insert the product Desk Lamp (category Furniture, price 35.0, stock 40). Add 8 to the stock of Standing Desk. Delete the product named Printer Ink.
starter:
-- 1. insert the lamp

-- 2. add the desks

-- 3. remove the ink
hint: UPDATE products SET stock = stock + 8 WHERE name = 'Standing Desk'; never forget the WHERE.
verify: SELECT name, category, price, stock FROM products ORDER BY name

title: A proper supplier table
brief: Our suppliers live in a spreadsheet that someone overwrote last month. I want them in the database, with rules so nobody can type a rating of 12 or a supplier twice.

skill.title: CREATE TABLE with rules
skill.card: Each column gets a type and optional constraints: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK (...) and REFERENCES other(id). The database then refuses bad writes from every app.
skill.example: SELECT name, type, "notnull", pk FROM pragma_table_info('products');

task: Create suppliers with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, city TEXT, rating INTEGER with a CHECK between 1 and 5, and product_id INTEGER referencing products(id). Then insert two suppliers: Bureau Plus, Lyon, rating 4, product 2; Tech Grossiste, Paris, rating 5, product 1.
hint: Use exactly those types: the checker compares column names, types, NOT NULL and the primary key.
verify: SELECT name, type, "notnull", pk FROM pragma_table_info('suppliers') ORDER BY cid
SELECT name, city, rating, product_id FROM suppliers ORDER BY name

title: A revenue view for the dashboard
brief: Our dashboard tool should not hold your joins in its config. Give me a view with revenue per sales rep that I can simply SELECT from, and an index so the order lookups by rep stay fast.

skill.title: Views save queries, indexes speed them up
skill.card: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ... stores a query under a name: it reads like a table and is always up to date. CREATE INDEX idx ON t(col) makes filters and joins on that column fast.

task: Create a view rep_revenue with columns rep (employee name) and revenue (sum of qty * unit_price, non cancelled orders, rounded to 2 decimals), one row per rep. Then create an index idx_orders_rep on orders(rep_id).
solution:
CREATE VIEW rep_revenue AS
SELECT e.name AS rep, ROUND(SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM employees e
JOIN orders o ON o.rep_id = e.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY e.id;
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_rep ON orders(rep_id);
hint: CREATE VIEW rep_revenue AS SELECT ... GROUP BY e.id; then CREATE INDEX idx_orders_rep ON orders(rep_id);
verify: SELECT name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index' AND name = 'idx_orders_rep'

title: Low stock alarm
brief: We ran out of whiteboards twice because nobody noticed. Whatever app changes the stock, I want the database itself to write an alert the moment a product drops under 5 units.

skill.title: Triggers react to changes
skill.card: CREATE TRIGGER t AFTER UPDATE OF col ON table WHEN cond BEGIN ... END; runs SQL by itself each time the table changes. Inside, OLD is the row before and NEW the row after.

task: Create stock_alerts(product_id INTEGER, stock INTEGER, raised_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) and a trigger low_stock that inserts product_id and the new stock whenever a product's stock is updated to a value below 5 that was 5 or more before. The checker will change some stock and read the alerts.
starter:
CREATE TABLE stock_alerts (product_id INTEGER, stock INTEGER, raised_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);

CREATE TRIGGER low_stock
hint: AFTER UPDATE OF stock ON products WHEN NEW.stock < 5 AND OLD.stock >= 5 BEGIN INSERT ... END;

title: A price change you can undo
brief: Last year an intern wiped the payments table and we spent a week rebuilding it. This time we test first: run the cleanup, look, undo it. Then the real job: services go up 5 percent, and that one stays.

skill.title: Transactions: all or nothing
skill.card: BEGIN opens a transaction. COMMIT makes every change since then permanent, ROLLBACK undoes them all. Wrap anything risky or anything that must happen together.

task: In one script: start a transaction, delete every row of payments, then ROLLBACK. Then in a second transaction raise the price of every Services product by 5 percent, rounded to 2 decimals, and COMMIT.
hint: BEGIN; DELETE ...; ROLLBACK; then BEGIN; UPDATE products SET price = ROUND(price * 1.05, 2) WHERE category = 'Services'; COMMIT;
verify: SELECT id, price FROM products ORDER BY id

title: The sales rep scorecard
brief: Board meeting on Friday. I want one table per sales rep: how many orders they closed, the revenue, how much of it is still unpaid, and their rank. Cancelled orders do not count anywhere. This is the report I will show, so make it right.

skill.title: Big reports are small steps
skill.card: Build the report in CTE steps: first one row per order, then one row per person, then rank with a window function. Each step is a query you can run and check alone.
skill.example: WITH ranked AS (SELECT name, dept_id, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn FROM employees) SELECT dept_id, name, salary FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

task: Return one row per rep who has orders: rep (name), orders (number of non cancelled orders), revenue (sum of qty * unit_price, rounded to 2 decimals), unpaid (revenue of their non cancelled orders that have no payment, rounded to 2 decimals, 0 when none) and sales_rank (RANK by revenue, highest = 1). Order by sales_rank.
starter:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.id, o.rep_id, SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price) AS total
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    GROUP BY o.id
)
SELECT * FROM order_totals;
solution:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.id, o.rep_id, SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price) AS total,
           NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.id) AS is_unpaid
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY o.id
), reps AS (
    SELECT e.name AS rep, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(t.total) AS revenue,
           SUM(CASE WHEN t.is_unpaid THEN t.total ELSE 0 END) AS unpaid
    FROM order_totals t
    JOIN employees e ON e.id = t.rep_id
    GROUP BY e.id
)
SELECT rep, orders, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue, ROUND(unpaid, 2) AS unpaid,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS sales_rank
FROM reps
ORDER BY sales_rank;
hint: CTE 1: one row per non cancelled order with its total and NOT EXISTS (payment) as a flag. CTE 2: group per rep, SUM(CASE WHEN flag THEN total ELSE 0 END). Then RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC).
